marble.name: Why We Have Seasons
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Explain that the seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis during its orbit around the Sun, distinguishing this from the common misconception that seasons are caused by changing distance from the Sun
marble.prompt: If you was asked why the UK is hot in summer but Australia is cold at the same time, could they explain that it's not about being closer to the Sun but about which half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun?

cluster.summary: Your child is discovering how daylight changes throughout the year by observing that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter.

misconceptions: Seasons are caused by Earth being closer to the Sun in summer and farther in winter (the dominant misconception; Earth is actually closest in January)
The whole Earth is warmer in summer at once (ignores that the hemispheres have opposite seasons simultaneously)
The axis tilts back and forth to point toward the Sun in summer (the axis direction is fixed; it is the orbital position that changes which hemisphere leans sunward)
Summer is warmer only because the days are longer (day length matters, but the directness/concentration of sunlight is the primary driver)
Tilt and 'the Sun being higher in the sky' are unrelated to how concentrated the sunlight is on the ground
representations: Tilted globe orbiting a central lamp with the axis fixed in direction (the canonical seasons model)
Torch-on-squared-paper demonstration of direct vs slanted light spreading over area (sunlight concentration)
Four-position orbit diagram (solstices and equinoxes) showing which hemisphere leans sunward
Side-by-side northern/southern hemisphere season labels at the same orbital instant
Sun-path / day-length graph across the year for a given latitude
authoredAnswer: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis (~23.5°). The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun receives more direct, concentrated sunlight and longer days = summer; the hemisphere tilted away gets slanted, spread-out light = winter. It can't be distance, because then both hemispheres would be warm or cold together — yet their seasons are opposite — and the Earth is in fact closest to the Sun during northern winter.
probe: Give the child a torch and squared paper in a dim room. Ask them to PREDICT with a reason: shining the torch straight down versus at a steep slant — same torch, same distance — will the lit patch look brighter, dimmer, or the same? wrongAnswers.wrong: Earth is closer to the Sun in summer and further away in winter.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: explains summer by the Earth being nearer the Sun
wrongAnswers.fix: If distance caused seasons the whole Earth would warm together — but it's summer in Australia during our winter, and Earth is closest in January. Tilt changes the ANGLE of sunlight, not the distance.

wrongAnswers.wrong: In summer your half of Earth is tilted nearer to the Sun, so it's closer.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: invokes tilt but explains it as being physically closer, not more directly lit
wrongAnswers.fix: The few thousand km of tilt is nothing against 150 million km — what matters is the ANGLE: overhead light is concentrated, slanted light is spread thin and weak.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: assumes everywhere on Earth shares one season at once
wrongAnswers.fix: Globe and lamp: as one hemisphere tilts sunward the other tilts away at the same moment — opposite seasons north and south.
